name: Iron Piston Doors
rationale:
Footprint Analysis
I am constructing a heavy mechanical installation known as the Iron Piston Doors. I will build this structure within a footprint that is 14 blocks wide along the X-axis, 15 blocks deep along the Z-axis, and 8 blocks tall along the Y-axis. Rather than a traditional hollow building, this structure is a dense, tiered mechanical housing. It transitions from a solid subterranean foundation to a complex mechanical core, framed by natural landscaping on one side, and topped with a heavy industrial casing. 

Material Strategy
I must choose my materials carefully to reflect both the mechanics and the environment. I will use Stone as the primary foundation and structural housing because it provides a sturdy, blast-resistant shell to protect the delicate machinery inside. I will use White Wool in the lower layers to map out the circuit paths and mechanical guides; wool is visually distinct and helps me organize the logic of the door's wiring. I will use Iron Blocks for the actual door panels, pistons, and heavy framing to give the entrance an impenetrable, industrial feel. Finally, I will use Dirt and Grass Blocks on the outer edges to blend the heavy machinery into the natural terrain, effectively hiding the subterranean mechanisms from the outside world.

Construction Sequence and Logic
At Y=0, I will lay down a completely solid 14 by 15 pad of Stone. I must do this to create the bedrock of my mechanism, ensuring that no underground caves or elements interfere with the door's operation. 

At Y=1, I will begin outlining the mechanical footprint. I will leave the front-left area open as an access trench. Along the right and back edges, I will build a Stone retaining wall. In the center, I will lay out a precise, symmetrical arrangement of Stone, White Wool, and Iron Blocks. I will use the White Wool here to act as my wiring paths, while the Iron Blocks will serve as the heavy anchor points for the pistons above.

At Y=2, I will build up the Stone walls to enclose the lower circuits. I should leave the center of this layer mostly hollow to allow the mechanical arms room to move and shift. I will place a few Iron Blocks to continue the vertical shafts rising from the anchors I placed in the layer below.

At Y=3, I will establish the surface level. On the front-left side, I will place Dirt topped with Grass Blocks to create a natural embankment, hiding the machinery below ground. On the back half, I will lay a thick slab of Stone to cover the rear mechanisms. In the center, I will construct a dense core of Iron Blocks. These represent the bases of the massive piston doors themselves.

At Y=4 and Y=5, I am building the actual sliding doors. I will leave the front and back areas completely open so that players can walk through the entrance. In the center, I will build two massive pillars of Iron Blocks, separated by a central gap. I will intersperse a few Stone blocks within the Iron to represent the piston heads and locking mechanisms holding the heavy doors in place.

At Y=6, I will cap the entire doorway with a heavy, solid canopy of Iron Blocks. I will build this as a massive lintel that acts as the upper track for the doors. This seals the mechanism from above and gives the structure a brutalist, highly secure appearance.

At Y=7, I will leave the layer entirely empty of machinery, except for a single Stone block in the far back-right corner. I will use this isolated block as a structural marker, perhaps as a mounting point for a future redstone torch, a security camera, or a structural tie-in for the rest of the mountain or wall this door will eventually connect to.
